newsitem.title: USA: Artist Willem De Kooning dies in New York.
newsitem.headline: Artist Willem De Kooning dies in New York.

text.p: Willem de Kooning, a founder of the Abstract Expressionist school that radically transformed American art in the 1940s, died Wednesday at age 92, an attorney for the de Kooning Conservatory said.

De Kooning, who stopped painting in 1990, had suffered in recent years from Alzheimer's disease and died of natural causes at his home and studio in East Hampton, New York, attorney John Silberman said.
The Dutch-born founder of Abstract Expressionism, strongly influenced by Arshile Gorky, Joan Miro and Pablo Picasso, painted abstract and figurative works with richly thick, masterful brush strokes.
With his first solo show mounted in 1948, de Kooning's black-and-white abstactions caused a critical stir and marked the birth of what would be coined Abstract Expressionism.
Soon an icon of American art, he would produce paintings that became more bright and airy, the whiplash lines replaced by long, stringy strokes traced several times in different hues.
"It's like being taken by the hand by a great dancer, the colour, the lyricism and the aliveness of everything," New York art critic Peter Schjeldahl said of de Kooning's work.

"He was the last great painter, for whom painting was a supreme mastery of all its technical aspects," he added. "There won't be any others. It's such an intensely complex set of skills that the whole culture has to be nurturing it."

Much of what followed -- Minimalism, Magic Realism, Deconstructionism, Op, Pop -- was a reaction to de Kooning'a style. His breakthrough paintings, done with ordinary house paint, were created at breakneck speed because, he said, the important thing was to "paint so fast you couldn't think."
One of his best known works is Woman I, painted in 1952.

Along with Jackson Pollock, with whom he had a friendly rivalry, de Kooning became a superstar of art in the 1950s and because of them, New York City became the centre of the art world. . "De Kooning cured America of its inferiority complex toward Europe," Schjedahl said. "America had a sense that we could never do it as well as Europe could, and de Kooning ended that."
The paintings that made de Kooning celebrated also made him rich. "Interchange," painted in 1955, sold for $20.8 million in 1989, when his body of work was estimated as being worth $300 million.

De Kooning was born on April 24, 1904, in Rotterdam, the Netherlands. His father was a beer distributor and his mother ran a bar. Employed by age 12 in a commercial art firm, he studied for eight years at Rotterdam's leading art school and came to the United States as a stowaway in 1926.
He worked as a carpenter and signpainter in New York City, then in 1935 landed a job with the Works Progress Administration, a government agency that employed artists during the Depression.

De Kooning's profound impact on the art world and generations of admiring artists to follow did not escape him, Schjeldahl said. He once said, in the days when there were bells on subway turnstiles, "When I go through there, I always expect the bells to ring a little bit louder."

In the 1960s, de Kooning began drawing figures with his eyes closed or by using his left hand. In 1981 he gave up drinking, a habit critics said had threatened his artistic skills. His last works, painted in the 1980s, are on exhibit at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City.
The works, painted as the artist was in deteriorating health, have come under some criticism for being what one critic called a "grim parody" of his life's achievement.
In his later years, de Kooning lived alone, with round-the-clock care.
He leaves a daughter, Lisa. His wife, artist Elaine de Kooning, died in 1989. The funeral is private, and a memorial will be announced later, the conservatory attorney said.
